# Leila Hormozi Voice Corpus

Research date: 2026-09-09

The excerpts below are short quotations from public YouTube transcripts and social posts, included under fair use for style analysis and attribution. They are third-party content and NOT covered by this repository's MIT license.

**Provenance note.** Item 1 was fetched directly from her personal LinkedIn profile on the research date and is verbatim, labeled `verified`. Items 2-30 come from auto-generated (ASR) YouTube caption tracks of her "Build with Leila" channel, confirmed `generated=True` via `yt.py tracks` on every video checked this session, and are labeled `documented` per the hard rule that ASR wording may be imperfect even when the ideas and phrasing are hers. Items 31-33 are `documented` from a search-snippet-only sighting of her X/Twitter account that could not be independently fetched (x.com returns HTTP 402 to automated fetch); treat with extra caution. Five of the eight ASR source videos were matched to a confirmed title and videoId by keyword search; two source files (leila-250m, leila-training) could not be matched to a specific videoId with confidence this session and are marked accordingly below.

**Punctuation note.** ASR captions carry little or no native punctuation. Minimal punctuation (periods, commas, capitalization) has been added for readability without changing, adding, or removing any word. No em dashes or en dashes were introduced; none appeared in the source material used.

## Documented (ASR transcripts, "Build with Leila" YouTube channel)

### From "How I Managed 120 Employees at Age 24 (Without Losing My Mind)" (YouTube, videoId 0gRQX9G45xo)

2. "If you lead your company with rules then you create rule followers. If you lead your company with values then you create leaders and people who can think."
   The operator's core argument for values over rules.

3. "Values give you a framework to make decisions that have not occurred yet."
   Named-concept definition, delivered flat.

4. "Lack of clear expectations leads to assumptions. Assumptions lead to unmet goals."
   Chained cause-and-effect, her default explanatory move.

5. "Expectations are the unsaid rules of engagement. They're actually non-negotiable agreed upon norms and behaviors that everyone on the team adheres to, but often are never verbalized, written, or explained."
   Definition-then-diagnosis pattern.

6. "If you don't properly define and verbalize your expectations, then nobody knows how to win or lose the game. They don't even know how to play the game."
   Game metaphor used to make an abstract management point concrete.

7. "A lot of bosses make the mistake of looking at a department that's underperforming and saying, oh gosh, I have to train this entire team on all this stuff. It's like no, you've got to train Jen. Jen sucks and she brings down the average of everybody."
   Named-example bluntness; the fix is the specific underperformer, not a training program.

8. "We've got three values. Unimpeachable character, sincere candor, competitive greatness."
   Her named framework, "the big three," repeated verbatim across multiple videos in this corpus.

9. "I realized that I was conflating responsibility with empathy. You can have empathy for somebody yet not take responsibility for their feelings."

10. "Guilt punishes ambition. So when you're ambitious, when you want things, and when you're achieving things, you feel bad if it makes other people feel bad."

### From "5 Signs to Fire Someone" (YouTube, videoId DxSyB1mOYkM)

19. "Fire someone if the employee repeatedly violates one of your big three values. For us, that's competitive greatness, sincere candor, unimpeachable character. After two documented conversations, fire them."
    Operational rule stated as a threshold, tied back to the named "big three."
    https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DxSyB1mOYkM

20. "Keep the person if the employee consistently demonstrates one of the big three, but lacks in skill. Keep them with some kind of clear measurable outcomes so you have a plan to get them better."
    Mirror-image rule to item 19; she always states the keep condition next to the fire condition.

21. "Fire them if they miss the same KPI or MIT two quarters in a row without any effort to improve."
    Numeric threshold as the decision rule.

22. "If it's a character issue, fire them fast. If it's a skill issue, coach harder. If they won't change, let them go. But if they're trying and they're improving, invest more in them."
    The closing binary that compresses the whole video into one rule.

## Structural notes for the writer

- She defines a term before she uses it, almost every time: recognition, accountability, sincere candor, suppression versus regulation. The definition is delivered flat, textbook-style, then she moves into the tactical breakdown.
- Numbered frameworks are load-bearing, not decorative: four levels of expectations, five signs to fire someone, five rules of leadership. She names the count out loud.
- She pairs a keep condition with a fire condition, a critique with an insult, suppression with regulation. Precision comes from splitting two things people conflate, not from a single strong claim.
- Personal disclosure (Alex, her marriage, her therapist, her own past failures) is used as proof, not as color. It always resolves into an operating rule.
- "The big three" (competitive greatness, sincere candor, unimpeachable character) and "chief accountability officer" are her named, repeated concepts. Credit them as hers; do not present them as generic advice.
